title: What, in your opinion, are some of the most "stylish" films of all time?

commenti.body: Blade Runner created it's own aesthetic and executed it perfectly. Fashion, architecture, cinematography - it all works. Style and world-building all together. I just watched it again yesterday, first time seeing the restored version and it was a mind-blowing experience, since I'd only seen the theatrical cut on crappy dvd prior to that.
[removed]

>Blade Runner created it's own aesthetic

Well no, it grafted a noir aesthetic onto a sci-fi premise.
[removed]

You've offered some questionable choices for the "stylish" moniker. I find Alex Garland's 'style' to be pretty non-existent, unless generic modern sci-fi is a 'style'. Ex Machina and Annihilation are solidly okayish films, but they don't have any identity of their own insofar as the cinematography, editing or sound design are concerned. 

A stylish film in my mind (which I take to mean aesthetically distinct but also showy) is something like Onibaba, The Night of the Hunter, Days of Heaven, Roma or A Girl Walks Home Alone at Night.
Wong’s Fallen Angels has to be the most stylish film ever made, with Chungking Express being a close second. I feel like I’d include Frances Ha and Inherent Vice on my list as well
[removed]

Tokyo Drifter, Branded to Kill, and many of Seijun Suzuki’s other films are some of the most stylish in film history. Largely because what makes them so memorable is purely the visual splendor, and gravitas he was bringing as a director for hire to the generic, mob-movie-of-the-week stories he was tasked with producing. Eventually Nikkatsu Company got so fed up with his surrealistic twists on scripts meant to be general audience money-makers that they fired him in 1967 after the release of Branded to Kill.
[removed]
[removed]

I'm going to clarify my definition of a "stylish film" upfront to give my answers some context.

To me, a stylish movie is one with a very distinct aesthetic where that aesthetic is one of the major themes. In other words, a movie whose appearance draws attention to itself as its own end, rather than primarily being a mechanism to address other themes. Also, I think "stylish" implies fashionable, high-end, visually sophisticated man-made environments and costumes in a generally urban setting.

So I wouldn't call *Lawrence of Arabia* "stylish" even though it has a fairly distinct and highly influential look, because the visuals are primarily meant to convey a story and sense of place rather than being thematic end goals in and of themselves. Nor would I call *The Wizard of Oz* "stylish" because even though the aesthetic is highly artificial and conspicuous, it is more weird and even kitschy than chic. 

Other people may define the term differenty. This is just my definition and it is intentionally narrow to avoid including just any movie whose cinematography or art direction I happen to like (which is essentially every film I like at all). 

So without further ado, here is a list of a few of my favorite "stylish" films:

* The Third Man (1949)
* Heat (1995)
* My Fair Lady (1964)
* The Grand Budapest Hotel (2014)
* Pierrot Le Fou (1965)
* A Star is Born (1954)
* The Red Shoes (1948)
* Bob Le Flambeur (1956)
* Sleeping Beauty (1959)

Pastiche is a major component of most innovation, though.

Prior to that film those two aesthetics were considered almost completely distinct, even oppositional. After that film, "noir futurism" became *the* default aesthetic for most sci-fi films set in cities. That is quite the accomplishment.
[removed]
[removed]

I agree entirely: I certainly wasn't trying to suggest fusing noir with sci-fi was a criticism of Blade Runner (notice my flair?)

When I think of films that "create their own aesthetic" however, the films which come to mind are not films which hybridise existing aesthetics connected to genre but those which try and create their own (though obviously nothing is truly original). Films like, I dunno, Fritz Lang's Sunrise or the films of the Dogme 95 movement.

Just personal choices:

Le Samourai

American Gigolo

In the Mood for Love 

The Neon Demon

Mahogany 

The Hunger

The Talented Mr. Ripley 

The Thomas Crown Affair - both versions 

Lola Montes

The Bitter Tears of Petra von Kant

Teorema

The Leopard 

Shaft

The Virgin Suicides

Boogie Nights

My point is that hybridization can be a novel aesthetic once it passes a certain threshold for innovation, which I think was the case with Blade Runner. You can't *easily* separate the components of that film's style into their original influences. Despite being a pastiche, the result is pretty coherent/homogeneous.

As for your counter-examples, I haven't seen Sunrise so I can't comment, but Dogme 95 films are mostly a blend of cinema verite and Italian neorealism. The filmmakers may have claimed to invented their style out of whole cloth, but I see a lot of hybridization going on there, as well.
Sunrise was directed by F.W. Murnau by the way, not Lang. (I had to google that to be sure fwiw)
Oh yes! My mistake.

>You can't easily separate the components of that film's style into their original influences. 

Yes you can! Noir narrative, sci-fi setting. Noir lighting, sci-fi soundscape. Noir archetypal characters, sci-fi themes. I am not saying these these things don't work together well: they complement each other wonderfully. But they're like hot fudge cake with vanilla ice-cream: just because they work together doesn't mean you can't tell which bit is which foodstuff.

>As for your counter-examples, I haven't seen Sunrise so I can't comment, but Dogme 95 films are mostly a blend of cinema verite and Italian neorealism. The filmmakers may have claimed to have invented their style out of whole cloth, but I see a lot of hybridization going on there, as well.

I don't think you've characterised Dogme 95 accurately there. They have elements of naturalism like those earlier movements you mentioned but they're also more weird and Brechtian.

All films have influence from what came before, nothing is truly original, but most films are not as easy to identify their genre elements as something like Blade Runner, which wears its genre conventions on its sleeve.

>Yes you can! 

A few of your examples kind of make sense, but I'd push back against others (e.g. sci-fit "setting" - the setting is a total mix of sci-fi and noir aesthetics). Moreover, you conventiently left out perhaps the most memorable aspect of the film's aesthetic after the cityscapes: the music. Which is 100% an amalgam of noir and sci-fi style. 

So no, I don't think separating out the infuences is super easy in all cases. The lighting is clearly noir-influenced. That one is pretty clear. The costumes are generally *either* noir (Deckard) *or* sci-fi (Pris). But many other elements of the film's style are fairly well-blended, namely the environment, the music, and even the themes/concepts.

>I don't think you've characterised Dogme 95 accurately there. They have elements of naturalism like those earlier movements you mentioned but they're also more weird and Brechtian.

Sure. Any successful/meaningful film style will be original in *some* way. But the influences in that filmmaking school are no less obvious to me than the influences on Blade Runner. 

>most films are not as easy to identify their genre elements as something like Blade Runner, which wears its genre conventions on its sleeve

Blade Runner is perhaps more obvious in this respect because it took two entire genres (not just a few films or filmmaking approaches) that already had very distinct aesthetics and which were very different from each other and then combined them together. That is a pretty unusual stylistic approach, no doubt. However, it's definitely a novel aesthetic on its own, just because it "works" so well. After seeing that film, it's almost hard to believe that no one thought of doing that before. It feels so natural in that movie's world.

>the setting is a total mix of sci-fi and noir aesthetics

True, insofar as it's LA. But futuristic LA, hence the 'noir done as a sci-fi film' approach.

>you conventiently left out perhaps the most memorable aspect of the film's aesthetic after the cityscapes: the music. Which is 100% an amalgam of noir and sci-fi style.

Does noir even have a music style? I've never really thought of noir films as having much musical identity, beyond the traditional Hollywood orchestral score you get in films of that period.

>it's definitely a novel aesthetic on its own, just because it "works" so well. After seeing that film, it's almost hard to believe that no one thought of doing that before. It feels so natural in that movie's world.

I agree.
[removed]

“Stylishness” and style are two different things in a film and not to be conflated. The Conformist is an example of stylishness over style. Oppenheimer even more so. In Barry Lyndon and other Kubrick what is normally seen as stylishness works as style as well.

Are the visuals of The Third Man or The Red Shoes really comparable to mannerism of something like The Grand Budapest Hotel though? The latter is what I’d describe as “stylish,” the other two where style properly bleeds into content

For me the best films, even "stylish" ones, marry form to content. So I would say the visuals of Grand Budapest Hotel serve the story and themes very well. It's just that they *also* call attention to themselves and are especially eye-catching and elaborate. 

As for the othe two films, I think the zither score in The Third Man is so conspicuous that it makes that film stylish by itself. And The Red Shoes qualifies for me due to the extended theatrical scene.

>But futuristic LA, hence the 'noir done as a sci-fi film' approach.

To me, most of the cityscape shots feature a scene so natural-looking that the parts (noir vs. sci-fi) are not immediately apparent.

Of course you *could* sit down and pick out the distinctions. But I don't think this occurs automatically for most viewers the way it would with an attempted fusion that didn't work.

>Does noir even have a music style?

Sort of...

I would say the most common perception is moody jazz.

But if you go back and watch most of the original films noir, they do mostly tend to have that orchestral/classical-inspired sound.

The Big Combo and some parts of Sweet Smell of Success might be closer to what people today think of as typical "noir" music. And especially Miles Davis' soundtrack for Elevator to the Gallows but that is a late entry in the classic period (1958).

Also, I think revisionist noirs had as much or more influence on the perceived noir sound than the originals (e.g. Chinatown - which I'm listening to atm and sounds the closest to the stereotype I can imagine).

So I don't know exactly how audiences perceived the soundtrack to Blade Runner when it first came out, but I think that melancholic, jazzy sound is closely linked to noir style in our consciousness today. It certainly isn't very sci-fi in most parts.

>I agree.

Oh good. We have reached common understanding. A rare feat indeed on this site.
